title: Combining word parts with context
blurb: Split an unfamiliar word into its parts, check every part against each option, and confirm the meaning with the sentence around it.
question: A TEAS item quotes a sentence: "After hours in the heat with no water, the hiker was dehydrated." One option says "overheated by the sun," which fits the sentence. Another says "lacking enough water." How do word parts and context work together to pick the right one?

teach.body: Formally, determining meaning from word parts means breaking a word into prefix, root (with any combining vowel) and suffix: the suffix often gives the part of speech or category, the root gives the core meaning and the prefix modifies it. Context then confirms. In plain English: the parts give you a rough translation, and the sentence checks it. The right answer agrees with every part of the word AND with the sentence.

teach.caption: Medical terms are usually read suffix first, then prefix, then root.

root.label: transdermal
root.sub: relating to passing through the skin

teach.caption: In 'The patch delivers medicine by a transdermal route,' the sentence confirms it: a patch works through the skin.

teach.body: Wrong options on the TEAS usually match ONE part of the word and contradict another. For bradycardia (brady- slow, cardi heart), 'fast heart rate' matches cardi but contradicts brady-, and 'heart pain' matches cardi but adds a pain suffix that is not there. Test each option against each part, and cross off any option that fails even one.

head: Option
hyper- (excessive)?

teach.caption: Only one option survives both checks.

teach.caption: The trap option names the right idea in the wrong form.
Inflammable means flammable: in- here does not mean 'not.'

teach.body: Sofia Hernandez, applying to a respiratory therapy program, reads: 'After hours in the heat with no water, the hiker was dehydrated.' She splits the word: de- (remove), hydr (water), -ate (verb) with -ed. Parts say: had water removed. Context agrees: no water for hours. She rejects 'overheated by the sun': it fits the heat in the sentence but nothing in the word means heat (that would be therm). Answer: lacking enough water.

teach.text: Three traps. (1) An option that fits the sentence but not the word parts, like 'overheated' for dehydrated. (2) An option that matches the root but ignores the prefix: hypoglycemia is LOW blood sugar. (3) The right idea in the wrong part of speech: a 'neurologist' is a person, not the study of nerves.

items: Split the word into prefix, root and suffix before reading the options.
Suffix = part of speech or category; root = core meaning; prefix = modifier.
The correct option agrees with every part; cross off any that fails one part.
Use context to confirm, and to settle double meanings such as in- and ped.
Beware options that fit the sentence but not the word.

summary: You can now break an unfamiliar word into its parts, test each answer option against every part, and confirm the meaning with context. You can also reject options that fit only the sentence, only one part, or the wrong part of speech.

A.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse used a hypodermic needle to give the vaccine." Based on its word parts, "hypodermic" means
A.why: Hypo- means below, derm means skin and -ic means relating to: relating to below the skin, which fits a needle used for a vaccine.

whyNot.1: Above would be supra- or epi-; hypo- means below.
whyNot.3: Inflammation would need -itis (dermatitis); hypo- means below.

A.q: Read the sentence: "After the fall, the chart noted bilateral knee pain." Based on its prefix, the patient has
A.why: Bi- means two, so bilateral means on both sides: pain in both knees.

whyNot.0: One side would be unilateral (uni- = one).
whyNot.1: Behind would be retro-, not bi-.
whyNot.3: Between would be inter-, not bi-.

A.q: Read the sentence: "Relief workers screened every child in the camp for malnutrition." Based on its word parts, "malnutrition" means
A.why: Mal- means bad and nutrition is nourishment: bad, or poor, nourishment.

whyNot.0: Excess would be hyper-; mal- means bad.
whyNot.2: Water is hydr; the base word here is nutrition.
whyNot.3: This matches mal- (bad) but ignores nutrition: the all-parts trap.

B.q: Read the sentence: "The doctor ordered a noninvasive test, so no needles or incisions were needed." In this context, "noninvasive" most nearly means
B.why: Non- means not, and the context (no needles or incisions) shows the test does not enter the body.

whyNot.0: This ignores non- and gives the opposite meaning.
whyNot.1: This ignores non-; a vein is ven or phleb, which is not in the word.
whyNot.2: This matches non- but contradicts the context: a doctor ordered the test.

B.q: Read the sentence: "Her frequent headaches led to a referral to a neurologist." Based on its word parts, a "neurologist" is
B.why: Neur means nerve and -logist means specialist: a person who specializes in nerves, which fits a referral.

whyNot.1: The study of nerves is neurology (-logy); -logist names the person.

B.q: Read the sentence: "After hours in the heat with no water, the hiker was dehydrated." Based on word parts and context, "dehydrated" means
B.why: De- means remove and hydr means water: water has been removed. The context (no water for hours) confirms it.

whyNot.1: This fits the heat in the sentence, but nothing in the word means heat (that would be therm).
whyNot.3: Urine would be ur or -uria, which is not in the word.

C.q: Read the sentence: "The test produced an electrocardiogram showing a normal rhythm." Based on its word parts, an "electrocardiogram" is
options: an instrument for hearing the heart
a record of the heart's activity
a procedure to view the heart
C.why: Cardi means heart and -gram means a record: a record of the heart's (electrical) activity, which fits 'showing a normal rhythm.'

C.q: Read the sentence: "Her doctor said the thinning of her bones was caused by osteoporosis." Based on its word parts, "osteoporosis" is
options: a tumor that forms in bone
C.why: Oste/o means bone and -osis means an abnormal condition, which fits the thinning bones in the sentence.

whyNot.0: Inflammation is -itis; -osis is an abnormal condition, not inflammation.

C.q: Read the sentence: "The sharp chest pain was caused by pericarditis." Based on its word parts, "pericarditis" means
C.why: Peri- means around, cardi means heart and -itis means inflammation: inflammation around the heart.

whyNot.1: Within would be endo- or intra-, not peri-.
whyNot.3: Beside is para-, the classic look-alike for peri-.

reteach.title: Be a detective with two witnesses
reteach.question: A detective trusts a story when two witnesses agree. How do word parts and context act as two witnesses to a word's meaning?

blocks.body: Witness one is the word itself: its prefix, root and suffix each give a piece of evidence. Witness two is the sentence around it. A suspect answer is cleared only when both witnesses agree. 'Overheated' satisfies the sentence about a hot hike but fails the word-parts witness for dehydrated, so it is ruled out.

rows.label: Catches
values: Options that fit the story only

blocks.text: One witness is not enough. An option that fits the sentence but not the word, or the word but not the sentence, is wrong.

explain.body: Break the word into prefix, root and suffix before reading the options. For medical terms, read the suffix first, then the prefix, then the root.

test.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse noted tachycardia when the patient's pulse reached 130 beats per minute." Based on its word parts, "tachycardia" is
test.why: Tachy- means fast and cardi means heart: a fast heart rate, which fits a pulse of 130.

whyNot.1: Pain would need -algia or -dynia; tachy- means fast.
whyNot.3: Tachy- refers to speed, not regularity of rhythm.

explain.h: Suffix sets the part of speech
explain.body: The suffix decides whether the answer is a person, a thing, a quality or an action. An option can name the right idea in the wrong form.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The clinic hired a physical ___ to help patients walk again."
test.why: The sentence needs a person who is hired. -ist names a person who does something: therapist.

whyNot.0: Therapy is the treatment, not the person hired.
whyNot.2: -ic forms an adjective, not a person.
whyNot.3: Therapies is the plural of the treatment, not a person.

explain.body: The correct option agrees with every part. Cross off any option that matches one part but contradicts or ignores another.

test.q: Read the sentence: "The monitor alarmed during each episode of apnea while the infant slept." Based on its word parts, "apnea" is
test.why: A- means without and -pnea means breathing: a period without breathing, which fits an alarm sounding.

explain.body: Some parts have two meanings. in- can mean not (inactive) or into (inhale); ped can mean foot or child. The sentence tells you which one applies.

test.q: Read the sentence: "The coach told the athletes to inhale slowly through the nose." In "inhale," the prefix in- means
test.why: Breathing air in through the nose is movement inward, so in- here means into.

whyNot.1: In- means not in words like inactive, but this sentence describes drawing air in, so here it means into.
